name: Welsh
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: Accent in native words falls on the penultimate syllable
sweep_summary: Welsh (wels1247) is in the catalog as fixed-strict penultimate, deciding quote 'Accent in native words falls on the penultimate syllable' (Watkins 1992 via StressTyp2), checked earlier against Morris-Jones 1913 and two open papers (Bell et al. JIPA 2021/2023; Mennen, Mayr & Morris ICPhS 2015, both held by the project). Of the 10 stress-titled bibliography items, six are Glottolog mis-tags (four records of Höhle's German 'normale Betonung' paper, Kuhn 1933 on Old Germanic, Struckmeier 2014 on German word order), one is a Welsh-English sociophonetic paper (Podhovnik 2010, downloaded and read; silent on Welsh word stress), one is medieval verse metrics (Davies 1928, paywalled, low priority), and two are genuinely about Welsh word stress: Watkins 1954 'The Accent in Cwm Tawe Welsh' (ZCP 24: 6-9, De Gruyter paywall) and Dogil & Williams 1999 Eurotyp chapter (Welsh section by Williams, De Gruyter paywall). Neither could be downloaded (De Gruyter bot-wall; Crossref records seen; no open copy on OpenAlex/S2/archive.org; In their place this search of works with stress in the title obtained and read the first-hand source behind both — Williams 1983 'Stress in modern Welsh', Cambridge PhD, open on the Apollo repository with a extracted text). It states (p. 23) that stress is fixed on the penult in polysyllables, exceptions nearly all final-stressed, antepenult only in recent English loans — confirming the catalog's classification — and it quotes Watkins 1954 pp. 8-9 verbatim (phonetic prominence often on the ultima in the Swansea Valley dialect; 'no great stress in modern Welsh'), which refines the phonetic picture without touching the location rule. Recommendation: replace the second-hand StressTyp2 deciding line with Williams 1983 §1.3.1 (or keep Morris-Jones 1913 §40) and add a caution that the ultima is often phonetically more prominent than the stressed penult (Williams 1983: 24-25; Watkins 1954: 9). written at covering all six files there.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Welsh is fixed on the penultimate syllable, for polysyllables. In the few cases where the stress does not follow this rule, nearly every example has stress on the final syllable. Only a very small minority of words have stress on a syllable before the penult; such words are mainly recent loans from English, and thus can perhaps be discounted as not being part of the native word-stock.
new_statements.citation: Williams, Briony Jane. 1983. Stress in modern Welsh. Ph.D. dissertation, University of Cambridge (Selwyn College / Department of Linguistics). Apollo repository,https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/250821
new_statements.locator: §1.3.1 'Welsh stress rule', p. 23 (p. 29); exceptions restated §3.8.2.1, p. 193 (p. 198): 'polysyllables stressed on the penult. There are some exceptions, but these are due either to direct borrowing from the English, or to historical syllable contraction, or to the presence of an unstressable proclitic as the penult.'
new_statements.reading: First-hand, dedicated experimental monograph on Welsh stress (acoustic measurements plus perception tests). States a fixed penultimate rule for polysyllables, with lexical exceptions almost all final-stressed (borrowings, historical contraction, unstressable proclitic penults) and antepenultimate stress only in recent English loans. This is exactly the catalog's fixed-strict penult coding (penultimate stress). Phonetic caveat (pp. 24-25, drawing on Watkins 1954 and D.M. Jones 1949): the ultima is often acoustically more prominent (higher pitch, longer) than the stressed penult, and stress is cued mainly by rhythm and post-stress consonant length; this is why non-Welsh listeners mis-hear stress as final. Does not affect the location rule.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (258 pp., Acrobat Paper Capture scanned layer; extracted text run directly on the PDF, no scanned needed). sources.quote: '... it would seem that the stress and pitch in modern Welsh especially in the Southern dialects are not on different syllables. The pitch has a tendency to follow the stress, but one thing is sure, and that is there is no great stress in modern Welsh. There is very little difference between the penultimate and final syllables, pitch and stress accents resting upon one or the other depending upon the position of a word in a sentence and the importance which is attached to the word. It is true to say, however, that the final syllable is longer (comparatively) than the penult and that this is a contributing factor in lending it greater clarity in dialect words' (Watkins 1953: 9)
sources.locator: Watkins 1954: 9 (and p. 8), as quoted in Williams 1983, pp. 24-25 (§1.3.2-1.3.3; pp. 30-31)
sources.note: Not obtainable (De Gruyter paywall; 405/202 bot-wall; no open copy located). Its content is quoted verbatim second-hand in Williams 1983 (pp. 24-25): a rudimentary acoustic study of the Swansea Valley dialect finding that the ultima has higher pitch than the penult and that greatest intensity/duration may fall on either penult or ultima; Watkins concludes there is 'no great stress in modern Welsh' and 'very little difference between the penultimate and final syllables'. This concerns phonetic prominence in one southern dialect and does not dispute the penultimate location of phonological word…
